title: Imamate of Yemen
capsule: The Zaydi Imamate of Yemen had existed since the ninth century but entered a prolonged reorganized phase from around 1814 under Imam al-Mahdi Abdallah, operating from the northern highlands while Ottoman, Wahhabi, and later Egyptian forces contested coastal Arabia. The imamate drew on the Zaydi Shia tradition requiring the imam to combine descent from the Prophet with personal legal scholarship and active leadership, giving the highland institution a theological distinctiveness from its Sunni neighbors. This particular phase of the imamate closed as renewed Ottoman expansion under the Tanzimat pressed into Yemen's northern regions during the 1870s, though the institution itself persisted in various forms until the republican revolution of 1962.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The territorial extent of this early nineteenth-century phase of the imamate is poorly attested; the highlands core is clear but boundaries against Ottoman and tribal zones are approximate.
